story.title: Could YOU Survive the Titanic?
story.topic: Could YOU Survive? Ep 1: in the North Atlantic at 2:20 AM, 15 April 1912, after the Titanic sank: water about -2 C, cold shock, ten minutes of useful arms, half-empty lifeboats, only Lifeboat 14 went back, chief baker Charles Joughin's two-hour survival and the whisky legend
story.angle: Second person: YOU are in the water; survival science second by second, a choice question for the comments, a twist (the baker) and a series hook
story.centralQuestion: How long would you last in -2 C water?
story.takeaway: Cold water kills fast: the first minute and the first ten minutes decide most of it
story.tone: tense, urgent, second person; wry twist
story.sensitivity: About 1,500 people died: no gore, no bodies; far swimmers are small, dignified silhouettes; the mascot carries the danger with expressions, never jokes about victims

claims.claim: RMS Titanic sank at about 02:20 ship's time on 15 April 1912.
Titanic carried 20 lifeboats (16 wooden, 4 collapsible) with room for about 1,178 people.
About 705-712 people survived; Carpathia picked up the survivors (Wikipedia gives 710; other tallies 705-712).

sources.title: House Divided / Dickinson: survivors variously given 705-708

claims.claim: Many lifeboats were launched partly empty: e.g. No. 7 left with about 27-28 people in a boat for 65; No. 2 with 25 of 40.

sources.title: Smithsonian Magazine: Photos of the Titanic tragedy from 101 years ago

claims.qualification: narration says 'many half empty' (approximate, not all boats)

claims.claim: The sea temperature that night was about -2 C (28 F), below freezing for fresh water (sea water freezes lower).

sources.title: Cruise Hive: How cold was the water when the Titanic sank?
Encyclopedia Titanica forum: Temperature of water

claims.qualification: commonly reported figure (28 F); some estimates differ, so narration says 'about minus two degrees'

claims.claim: Sudden immersion in cold water triggers the cold-shock response: an involuntary gasp and hyperventilation in roughly the first minute; a gasp with the head under water can inhale water and drown.

sources.title: Canadian Safe Boating Council: the 1-10-1 principle

claims.claim: The 1-10-1 rule: about 1 minute of cold shock, about 10 minutes of meaningful movement before the muscles of the arms and legs fail, about 1 hour before unconsciousness from hypothermia; the timings vary and are shorter in colder water.

sources.title: Canadian Safe Boating Council: the 1-10-1 principle

claims.qualification: memory aid, not a stopwatch: narration says 'Ten minutes, maybe less'

claims.claim: Lifeboat No. 14, under Fifth Officer Harold Lowe, is described as the only lifeboat to go back to search for survivors after the sinking; it pulled a few people from the water (about four, one of whom died).

sources.title: US Senate Inquiry: testimony of Harold Lowe

claims.qualification: some accounts count Lifeboat 4 (picked up swimmers close by) as a second; narration: 'Only one comes back: Lifeboat fourteen' follows Wikipedia's wording

claims.claim: Charles Joughin, the ship's chief baker, testified that he was in the water for over two hours and survived, holding on to Collapsible B and later taken into another lifeboat.

sources.title: Tim Maltin: Titanic Chief Baker Charles Joughin survived for several hours in the freezing water

claims.qualification: his own account, uncorroborated; historians think his head and upper body stayed out of the water: narration says 'said he lasted about two hours'

claims.claim: Legend says whisky saved Joughin; in his testimony he spoke of a drink of liqueur; scientists say alcohol does not protect against cold water (it can speed heat loss).

sources.title: Tim Maltin: Titanic Chief Baker Charles Joughin survived for several hours in the freezing water

claims.qualification: framed as legend; 'Scientists doubt it helped'

claims.claim: The ship's lights failed shortly before the final plunge (about 2:18 AM), and the hull broke apart between the third and fourth funnels; the stern rose high before sinking.
claims.qualification: picture only (the stern lights flicker out in shot 1)

claims.claim: The night was calm, clear, cold and moonless, with a sky full of stars.
Titanic's fourth (aft) funnel was a dummy used mainly for ventilation.
'Joughin was drunk out of his mind and that is why he survived.'

sources.title: Tim Maltin: Titanic Chief Baker Charles Joughin survived for several hours in the freezing water

claims.qualification: NOT USED: Maltin calls it a myth; Joughin said he was not drunk

weaknesses.issue: -2 C (28 F) is the commonly reported figure; some estimates differ: narration says 'about'.
'Only one comes back' follows Wikipedia (Lifeboat 14); some accounts also count Lifeboat 4 picking up swimmers nearby.
Joughin's two hours is his own uncorroborated testimony; framed as 'said he lasted'. Whisky framed as legend (he testified to liqueur).
Voice runs 39.9 s (86 words) because the ElevenLabs quota ran out before the planned 80-word take; total 41.9 s with the end card (target 35-40).
Picture shows the stern lights on at 2:20; the lights actually failed about 2:18, so the stern's lights flicker out in shot 2.

publishing.description:
It's 2:20 AM on 15 April 1912. The Titanic has just gone under, and YOU are in the North Atlantic. The water is about −2 °C (28 °F).

What happens to your body, second by second:
• The first minute: cold shock. You gasp and hyperventilate without meaning to; a gasp under a wave can make you inhale water.
• About 10 minutes (often less in water this cold): your arm and leg muscles stop working, so you can no longer swim or hold on well (the "1-10-1" rule: about 1 minute, 10 minutes, 1 hour; it is a memory aid, not a stopwatch).
• Titanic carried 20 lifeboats with room for about 1,178 people, and many were launched partly empty (Lifeboat 7 left with about 28 people in a boat for 65). About 1,500 people died; about 705-712 survived.
• Lifeboat 14, under Fifth Officer Harold Lowe, is described as the only boat that went back to search for survivors. It pulled a few people from the water.
• The twist: chief baker Charles Joughin said he spent over two hours in the water and lived. Legend says whisky saved him; in his own testimony he spoke of a drink of liqueur, and scientists doubt alcohol helped (it makes you lose heat faster). Historians think he kept his head and upper body out of the water, with his life jacket.

Episode 2: Pompeii. Follow so you don't miss it.

Sources:
- Wikipedia, Sinking of the Titanic (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinking_of_the_Titanic)
- Wikipedia, Titanic Lifeboat No. 14 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanic_Lifeboat_No._14)
- Wikipedia, Charles Joughin (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Joughin)
- Tim Maltin, Titanic chief baker Charles Joughin (https://timmaltin.com/2019/05/07/joughin-baker-titanic/)
- US Senate Inquiry, testimony of Harold Lowe (https://www.titanicinquiry.org/USInq/AmInq05Lowe02.php)
- Canadian Safe Boating Council, the 1-10-1 principle (https://csbc.ca/1-10-1-principle/)
- Smithsonian Magazine, Photos of the Titanic tragedy (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/photos-of-the-titanic-tragedy-from-101-years-ago-19446446/)
